mappings.note: Names ruminants as the group of animals that chew the cud: organisms placed in a class by a shared feature.
Names the gizzard as the grinding organ birds have in place of teeth: a part identified by its role.
Names respiration as the release of energy from glucose using oxygen. Not LO-119, because no word equation is written.
Names breathing as the physical taking in and letting out of air, the process set against respiration elsewhere.
Names absorption as nutrients passing from gut into blood, a stage of the process.
Villi increasing the surface for absorption: how the organ is built to do its job, which is part of explaining the process.
Celiac disease as a reaction to gluten that damages the intestine: health knowledge that bears on what a person can eat, so the day-to-day outcome.
The large intestine as the next part after the small intestine: the order of organs along the canal.
The large intestine absorbing water and salts: what that organ does in the process.
Names stool as the semi-solid waste the large intestine forms, the product of the last stage.
The rectum as the store for stool before it leaves: a part identified by position and role.
The stem, complete with its own answer, is again the rectum question, so it is mapped on that; the printed answer field belongs to a breathing item and is reported as a defect.
Ribs down and in with the diaphragm relaxing upwards during exhalation: the mechanism of breathing out.
The balloons in the bottle model stand for the lungs: reading the model that was built from everyday materials.
The rubber sheet stands for the diaphragm, the companion part of the same model.
What the two lime water tubes show about exhaled air: a conclusion drawn from the experimental comparison.
Gas exchange happening across the alveolar walls: the step of the process, not merely the name of the sac.
About twenty-one per cent oxygen in inhaled air, a fact about the air the process works on.
The small fraction of carbon dioxide in inhaled air, the companion figure.
Names inhalation as taking air in, one half of the breathing process.
Names the alveoli as the tiny air sacs of the lungs.
Names the diaphragm, the dome-shaped muscle below the lungs.
Defines digestion and says why animals need it: the purpose of the process.
Teeth breaking food up as mechanical digestion, the first stage of the process.
Saliva moistening food and starting starch breakdown: its part in the process.
Wave-like contractions carrying food to the stomach, the transport mechanism.
Acid and mucus in the stomach described together, both as functional steps.
Bile from the liver and juice from the pancreas and what each does: the role of the two glands in digestion. The item that merely names them is on LO-113.
How the small intestine is fitted for absorption, through length and villi: structure explained in terms of the process.
Water and salt absorption turning the residue into stool: the large intestine's part of the process.
Explains rumination from first chewing through the rumen to re-chewing the cud.
Breathing against respiration, the mechanical act against the chemical release of energy: both processes explained.
The stem, again self-answering, is the breathing-and-respiration question and is mapped on that; the printed answer field belongs to a small-intestine item and is reported as a defect.
The diaphragm changing the volume of the chest cavity: its function within the breathing mechanism.
Matches the alveoli to gas exchange among four respiratory parts: parts identified by their functions.
Why we inhale air rich in oxygen rather than oxygen itself: accuracy about what the breathing process takes in.
Faster breathing after running traced to the extra oxygen needed and carbon dioxide produced: effect tied to cause.
Names one of the life processes, which is picking a member of the category.
Names the alimentary canal.
Digestion beginning in the mouth: where the process starts.
Saliva as what acts on starch in the mouth, a step of the process.
Starch as the nutrient saliva begins to digest, the other half of the same step.
Names the food pipe between mouth and stomach.
Acid as the stomach secretion that kills bacteria: a secretion named by what it does.
Mucus as the secretion that shields the lining, the companion functional item.
